title: Immunology
summary: Innate and adaptive immunity, and what happens when they misfire.

lessons.title: Innate Immunity

levels.kid:
Your body has a security team that is always on duty. This team is called **innate immunity**. It is the first to show up when germs sneak in.

Your skin is like a castle wall. Tears, spit and the slime in your nose trap germs and wash them away.

If germs get past the wall, special cells rush in. Some of them are **eaters**. They gobble germs up like a vacuum cleaner.

The area might get red, warm, puffy and sore. That is called **inflammation**. It looks annoying, but it means your guards are fighting.

This team is fast, but it does not learn. It treats every germ about the same way, every single time.
levels.hs:
**Innate immunity** is the body's built-in, fast, non-specific defense. It works within minutes to hours, responds the same way every time, and does not form memory.

It has several layers:
- **Physical and chemical barriers**: skin, mucous membranes, cilia that sweep mucus out of the airways, stomach acid, and enzymes like **lysozyme** in tears and saliva.
- **Phagocytes**: cells that eat microbes. **Neutrophils** are the most common white blood cell and arrive first. **Macrophages** are larger, live longer, and also clean up debris.
- **Natural killer (NK) cells** destroy virus-infected cells and some tumor cells.
- **The complement system**: blood proteins that coat microbes so they are easier to eat, attract more cells, and punch holes in bacteria.
- **Fever**, which slows some microbes and speeds up immune responses.

When tissue is invaded, **inflammation** follows, with the classic signs of redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Blood vessels widen and become leaky so cells and proteins can reach the problem.

Innate cells recognize patterns that are common to many microbes, such as parts of bacterial cell walls. They also alert the adaptive immune system, which takes days to get going but is precise.
levels.college:
Innate immunity is germline-encoded and recognizes conserved microbial structures called **PAMPs** (pathogen-associated molecular patterns: LPS, peptidoglycan, flagellin, unmethylated CpG DNA, viral double-stranded RNA) and host danger signals called **DAMPs** (HMGB1, ATP, uric acid crystals) using **pattern recognition receptors (PRRs)**.

Key PRR families:
- **Toll-like receptors (TLRs)**: TLR4 detects LPS of Gram-negative bacteria; TLR2 lipoproteins and lipoteichoic acid; TLR5 flagellin; TLR3, 7, 8 and 9 sit in endosomes and sense nucleic acids. Signaling through MyD88 and TRIF activates **NF-kB** and IRFs, producing inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) and type I interferons.
- **NOD-like receptors** form **inflammasomes**, which activate caspase-1 to cleave pro-IL-1 beta and pro-IL-18 into active forms.
- **RIG-I-like receptors** and **cGAS-STING** sense viral RNA and cytosolic DNA.

**Complement** has three activation routes: classical (antibody bound to antigen, C1q), lectin (mannose-binding lectin), and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis on microbial surfaces). All converge on **C3 convertase**. Effector functions: **C3b** opsonization, **C3a and C5a** as anaphylatoxins and chemoattractants (C5a especially), and the **membrane attack complex (C5b-9)**, which is critical against Neisseria.

**Neutrophil recruitment** proceeds in steps: selectin-mediated rolling, integrin activation (LFA-1 binding ICAM-1), firm adhesion, diapedesis, then chemotaxis toward IL-8, C5a, LTB4 and bacterial peptides. Killing uses the oxidative burst (NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase producing hypochlorite) and granule enzymes, plus NETs.

**NK cells** kill cells that lack MHC class I ('missing self'), using perforin and granzymes, and are activated by IL-12.

**Acute-phase response**: IL-6 drives the liver to make CRP, fibrinogen and ferritin, while IL-1 and TNF act on the hypothalamus to produce fever.
levels.phd:
The old picture of innate immunity as primitive and memoryless has been revised on several fronts.

First, **trained immunity**: monocytes and NK cells exposed to beta-glucan or BCG vaccine show enhanced responses to unrelated pathogens for months. The mechanism is epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow (H3K4me3 marks at inflammatory gene promoters, a shift toward aerobic glycolysis via mTOR and HIF-1 alpha). This may partly explain the non-specific mortality benefits of some live vaccines in epidemiological studies, though causality is debated.

Second, **innate lymphoid cells (ILC1, ILC2, ILC3)** mirror helper T cell subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17) but lack antigen receptors. ILC2s sit in barrier tissues and respond to epithelial alarmins (IL-33, IL-25, TSLP), driving type 2 inflammation in asthma before any T cell gets involved.

Third, the decision to inflame is layered. The NLRP3 inflammasome typically needs two signals: priming (NF-kB induced transcription of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1 beta) and activation (potassium efflux, crystals, mitochondrial damage). Caspase-1 also cleaves **gasdermin D**, whose N-terminal fragment forms membrane pores and causes **pyroptosis**, an inflammatory cell death. Gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations cause cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, a classic **autoinflammatory** disease: episodic fever and inflammation without autoantibodies or autoreactive T cells.

Fourth, innate sensing instructs adaptive immunity. Dendritic cells integrate PRR signals into costimulatory molecule expression and cytokines that polarize T cells. This is the logic of **vaccine adjuvants**: alum activates NLRP3-related pathways, while newer adjuvants are TLR agonists (TLR4 agonist MPL, TLR9 agonist CpG).

Finally, the cost of innate immunity is collateral damage. Sepsis is less a failure to kill microbes than a dysregulated host response, with early hyperinflammation and later immunoparalysis, which is one reason simple anti-cytokine strategies have repeatedly failed in trials.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, innate immunity shows up in three ways: how infection presents, how you read the labs, and what you suspect when it fails.

**Presentation**: a neutropenic patient can have a serious bacterial infection with very little pus, minimal infiltrate on chest X-ray and no meningismus, because neutrophils produce much of the inflammation we look for. Fever in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count below 500 per microliter is an emergency: blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour, without waiting for a source.

**Labs**: CRP rises within hours and falls quickly with treatment, so a trend is more useful than a single value. Procalcitonin rises more in bacterial than viral infection and can support stopping antibiotics, but it is not perfect (it rises after trauma or surgery). A left shift (bands) and toxic granulation point toward bacterial infection. Remember that steroids cause neutrophilia by demargination, which can mimic infection.

**Failure patterns**:
- Recurrent **Neisseria** infections (meningococcal meningitis more than once, disseminated gonorrhea): check terminal complement (CH50); also counsel meningococcal vaccination for patients on terminal complement inhibitors such as eculizumab.
- Recurrent abscesses with catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia): think **chronic granulomatous disease**; the dihydrorhodamine flow test is the screen.
- Delayed umbilical cord separation and infections without pus: **leukocyte adhesion deficiency**.
- Severe herpesvirus infections: consider NK cell defects.

**Neurosurgical relevance**: the brain has its own innate cells, microglia, and the blood-brain barrier limits complement and neutrophil access. Postoperative fever in the first 48 hours is usually not infection; a wound or shunt infection days later, often with skin flora such as Staph epidermidis forming biofilm on hardware, is a different story and often needs the hardware removed.

Distinguish **autoinflammatory** disease (innate, periodic fevers, no autoantibodies) from autoimmune disease; the first responds to IL-1 blockade.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast, non-specific and has no classic memory
Barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement and fever are its main tools
PRRs like TLRs recognize PAMPs (TLR4 = LPS)
C3b opsonizes, C5a recruits neutrophils, C5b-9 forms the MAC (Neisseria)
Neutropenic fever is an emergency because signs of infection can be blunted

test.q: Which cell is usually the first white blood cell to arrive at a site of acute bacterial infection?
test.explain: Neutrophils dominate the first hours of acute inflammation. Plasma cells and memory T cells are adaptive and arrive much later.

test.q: What does TLR4 recognize?
choices: Unmethylated CpG DNA from bacteria and viruses (TLR9)
Viral double-stranded RNA made during replication (TLR3)
Flagellin from the tails of motile bacteria (TLR5)
test.explain: TLR4 binds LPS. Flagellin is TLR5, dsRNA is TLR3, CpG DNA is TLR9.

test.q: Which complement fragment is the main opsonin?
test.explain: C3b coats microbes so phagocytes can eat them. C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins; C1q starts the classical pathway.

test.q: Deficiency of C5–C9 (the membrane attack complex) especially predisposes to recurrent infection with:
test.explain: The MAC is important for killing Neisseria; terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent meningococcal and gonococcal disease.

test.q: NK cells kill target cells that:
choices: Lack or have reduced MHC class I
Display too much MHC class I
test.explain: NK cells use 'missing self': loss of MHC class I, common in virus-infected and tumor cells, removes an inhibitory signal.

test.q: Which is NOT a classic sign of inflammation?
test.explain: The cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Jaundice is a sign of bilirubin buildup.

test.q: Which cytokine drives the liver to produce CRP in the acute-phase response?
test.explain: IL-6 is the main inducer of hepatic acute-phase proteins like CRP.

test.q: The enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial cell walls is:
test.explain: Lysozyme cleaves peptidoglycan, especially in Gram-positive walls.

test.q: Which feature describes innate immunity?
choices: Takes about a week to begin
Highly specific receptors made by gene rearrangement
test.explain: Innate immunity is fast and uses germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors; specificity and classic memory belong to adaptive immunity.

test.q: What is the general name for conserved microbial molecules recognized by innate receptors? (abbreviation)
test.explain: PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) such as LPS and flagellin are recognized by PRRs like TLRs.

test.q: The inflammasome activates caspase-___ to produce active IL-1β.
test.explain: Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta and pro-IL-18; it also cleaves gasdermin D to trigger pyroptosis.

test.q: Which phagocyte enzyme complex produces the oxidative burst and is defective in chronic granulomatous disease?
test.explain: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide; its absence causes chronic granulomatous disease with catalase-positive infections.

test.q: Complement fragment C5___ is a powerful chemoattractant for neutrophils.
test.explain: C5a (and C3a) are anaphylatoxins; C5a especially attracts neutrophils.

kidTest.q: What is your body's first wall against germs?
kidTest.explain: Your skin is like a castle wall that keeps germs out.

kidTest.q: What do 'eater' cells do?
kidTest.explain: Eater cells (phagocytes) swallow germs.

kidTest.q: A cut gets red, warm and puffy. What is happening?
choices: You are growing a brand new skin
Nothing at all, it's totally normal
Your skin is slowly melting away
kidTest.explain: Redness, warmth and swelling mean your immune guards are at work.

kidTest.q: Does the innate team learn and remember germs?
choices: No, it acts the same every time
kidTest.explain: The innate team is fast but does not learn. The adaptive team remembers.

kidTest.q: Which of these traps germs in your nose?
kidTest.explain: Mucus is sticky and traps germs.

kidTest.q: Fill in: the always-ready guard team is called ___ immunity.
kidTest.explain: Innate immunity is the fast team that is always on duty.

advancedTest.q: A child has delayed umbilical cord separation and recurrent skin infections with no pus. Most likely defect?
advancedTest.explain: LAD type 1 (CD18 defect) prevents neutrophils from leaving vessels, so there is neutrophilia in blood but no pus in tissue.

advancedTest.q: Gasdermin D cleavage by caspase-1 leads to:
choices: Pyroptosis, an inflammatory cell death with membrane pores
MHC class I upregulation on the infected cell surface
Apoptosis without inflammation, via caspase-3 activation
Class switching in B cells from IgM to IgG antibodies
advancedTest.explain: The gasdermin D N-terminal fragment forms pores, releasing IL-1 beta and causing pyroptosis.

advancedTest.q: Periodic fevers and inflammation with no autoantibodies that respond to IL-1 blockade suggest:
advancedTest.explain: Autoinflammatory syndromes (e.g. cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes) come from innate pathways such as NLRP3 gain of function.

advancedTest.q: Trained immunity is best explained by:
choices: Epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of myeloid cells
advancedTest.explain: Trained immunity relies on epigenetic marks and metabolic shifts in innate cells and their bone marrow progenitors.

lessons.title: Adaptive Immunity: T and B Cells

levels.kid:
Your body has a second security team called **adaptive immunity**. This team is slower, but it is very smart.

It has two kinds of helpers. **B cells** make **antibodies**. Antibodies are like sticky tags that grab one exact germ so other cells can find it.

**T cells** are the bosses and the fighters. Helper T cells tell everyone what to do. Killer T cells find sick cells and get rid of them.

The best part is memory. After the team beats a germ, it keeps a 'wanted poster' of it. If that germ comes back, the team wins super fast, and you may not even feel sick.

That is how vaccines work: they show your body the wanted poster early.
levels.hs:
**Adaptive immunity** is slower to start (days) but highly **specific**, and it creates **memory**, so the second response to the same microbe is faster and stronger.

It relies on **lymphocytes**:
- **B cells** mature in the bone marrow. When activated, they become **plasma cells** that secrete **antibodies** (immunoglobulins). Antibodies neutralize toxins and viruses, tag microbes for phagocytes, and activate complement. This is **humoral** immunity.
- **T cells** mature in the **thymus**. **CD4 helper T cells** coordinate the response by releasing cytokines and helping B cells. **CD8 cytotoxic T cells** kill infected or cancerous cells. This is **cell-mediated** immunity.

T cells cannot see free-floating germs. They recognize small pieces of protein (**antigens**) displayed on **MHC** molecules (called HLA in humans). CD4 cells look at MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells; CD8 cells look at MHC class I, found on almost every cell.

There are five antibody classes: **IgM** (first made), **IgG** (most common in blood, crosses the placenta), **IgA** (in mucus, tears and breast milk), **IgE** (allergy and parasites) and **IgD**.

**Vaccines** create memory without the disease. Passive immunity, such as a mother's IgG reaching her baby, gives temporary protection with no memory.
levels.college:
**Generating diversity**: B and T cell receptors are assembled by **V(D)J recombination**, driven by RAG1 and RAG2 enzymes, with junctional diversity from TdT adding nucleotides. This creates millions of receptor specificities before any antigen is seen.

**Selection**: in the thymus, T cells undergo **positive selection** in the cortex (must bind self-MHC weakly) and **negative selection** in the medulla (strongly self-reactive cells die). **AIRE** lets medullary epithelial cells express tissue-specific self proteins. Some self-reactive CD4 cells become **regulatory T cells (Tregs)**, defined by **FOXP3**.

**Antigen presentation**:
- MHC I (HLA-A, B, C) presents cytosolic peptides loaded in the ER via TAP, to CD8 cells.
- MHC II (HLA-DR, DP, DQ) presents peptides from endocytosed proteins, after the invariant chain is removed, to CD4 cells.
- Dendritic cells can **cross-present** exogenous antigen on MHC I.

**T cell activation** needs signal 1 (TCR plus MHC-peptide), signal 2 (costimulation, B7 on the APC binding CD28), and cytokines (signal 3). Signal 1 without signal 2 leads to anergy. **CTLA-4** and **PD-1** are inhibitory checkpoints.

**CD4 subsets**: Th1 (IFN-gamma, activates macrophages, intracellular microbes), Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13: IgE, eosinophils, helminths), Th17 (IL-17: neutrophils, extracellular bacteria and fungi), Tfh (help B cells in germinal centers), Treg (IL-10, TGF-beta).

**B cell responses**: T-dependent responses in germinal centers produce **class switching** (requires CD40L on T cells binding CD40 on B cells, and AID) and **affinity maturation** by somatic hypermutation. T-independent antigens (polysaccharide capsules) give mostly IgM and weak memory, which is why conjugate vaccines link polysaccharide to a protein carrier.

**Primary vs secondary response**: IgM peaks first in a primary response; secondary responses are faster, larger and dominated by high-affinity IgG.
levels.phd:
Adaptive immunity solves a statistical problem: how to recognize an unpredictable universe of antigens with a finite genome while avoiding self-attack. The answer is somatic diversification followed by selection, a Darwinian process inside the body.

The theoretical TCR repertoire exceeds 10^15 possible receptors, but a human holds roughly 10^11 T cells with perhaps 10^7 to 10^8 distinct clonotypes. Repertoire sequencing shows a power-law distribution: a few large clones (often against CMV) and a long tail of rare ones. **Cross-reactivity** is unavoidable and essential: a single TCR can recognize over a million distinct peptides, which is how a limited repertoire covers a vast space, and also a route to molecular mimicry.

Tolerance is probabilistic, not absolute. Negative selection is incomplete, so the periphery depends on Tregs, anergy, and ignorance (antigen sequestered or below threshold). The **affinity threshold** model and kinetic proofreading explain how a T cell discriminates ligands differing subtly in dwell time.

Germinal centers are evolutionary engines. B cells cycle between the dark zone (proliferation, AID-driven somatic hypermutation) and the light zone (competition for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and for Tfh help). Affinity rises over weeks. AID's off-target activity explains translocations in B cell lymphomas (MYC to IgH in Burkitt lymphoma).

Memory is heterogeneous: central memory T cells in lymph nodes, effector memory cells in circulation, and **tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm)** that never leave barrier sites such as skin and lung and provide immediate local defense. Long-lived plasma cells in bone marrow niches maintain antibody titers for decades without antigen.

Immunological imprinting ('original antigenic sin') shows that prior exposures shape responses to related variants, as with influenza and SARS-CoV-2, a central consideration in vaccine strain design.
levels.expert:
Clinicians use adaptive immunity daily, mostly through serology, vaccination and immunomodulation.

**Serology logic**: IgM suggests recent infection; IgG implies past infection or vaccination. A fourfold rise in IgG titer between acute and convalescent samples supports a current infection. For hepatitis B, anti-HBs means immunity, anti-HBc IgM means acute infection, and isolated anti-HBc needs interpretation. Neonatal IgG mostly comes from the mother, so an infant's IgG result can reflect maternal antibody; IgM does not cross the placenta and points to fetal infection.

**Vaccination**: live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella) are generally avoided in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy. Conjugate vaccines (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal) work in infants because they recruit T cell help. Asplenic patients need vaccination against encapsulated organisms; for elective splenectomy, vaccinate beforehand.

**Transplant and HLA**: matching and crossmatching prevent antibody-mediated rejection. Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) block IL-2 transcription in T cells; their toxicities include nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity, including posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

**Monoclonal antibodies** exploit specificity: rituximab depletes CD20 B cells (watch for hepatitis B reactivation and, rarely, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from JC virus); natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin trafficking into the CNS for multiple sclerosis and carries a well-known PML risk, managed with JC virus antibody testing.

**Checkpoint inhibitors** (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) unleash T cells against tumors but cause immune-related adverse events: colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, myocarditis, and neurologic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis and encephalitis. New headache and fatigue on ipilimumab should prompt a check for hypophysitis.

**CNS relevance**: the CNS is not truly immune-privileged; meningeal lymphatics drain to deep cervical nodes. CAR-T cell therapy can cause immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), monitored with a bedside handwriting and attention score.

keyPoints: Adaptive immunity is specific, slower at first, and forms memory
B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral immunity)
CD4 T cells see MHC II; CD8 T cells see MHC I
IgM comes first, IgG crosses the placenta, IgA guards mucosa, IgE handles allergy and parasites
Class switching needs CD40L; T cell activation needs costimulation

test.q: Where do T cells mature?
test.explain: T cells develop in the thymus; B cells mature in the bone marrow.

test.q: CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize antigen presented on:
test.explain: CD8 binds MHC class I, which almost every nucleated cell expresses. CD4 pairs with MHC class II.

test.q: Which antibody crosses the placenta?
test.explain: IgG is transported across the placenta via the neonatal Fc receptor, giving the newborn passive immunity.

test.q: Which antibody is the first made in a primary response?
test.explain: IgM appears first; IgG follows after class switching.

test.q: The main antibody in mucus, tears and breast milk is:
test.explain: Secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces.

test.q: Which helper T cell subset drives IgE and eosinophils against parasites?
test.explain: Th2 cells release IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, promoting IgE class switching and eosinophils.

test.q: Signal 1 without costimulation (signal 2) causes a T cell to become:
test.explain: Without B7-CD28 costimulation, T cells become anergic (unresponsive), a tolerance mechanism.

test.q: Regulatory T cells are defined by the transcription factor:
test.explain: FOXP3 defines Tregs; mutations cause IPEX syndrome. AIRE works in thymic epithelium.

test.q: Why are conjugate vaccines used for polysaccharide-capsule bacteria in infants?
choices: They work without B cells, using T cells alone to kill bacteria
Linking to a protein recruits T cell help for strong memory
They contain live bacteria that colonize the infant's throat
They avoid needles by being absorbed through the skin instead
test.explain: Pure polysaccharides are T-independent antigens with weak memory in infants; protein conjugation recruits helper T cells.

test.q: Class switching from IgM to IgG requires CD40 on B cells to bind:
choices: CD40 ligand on helper T cells
MHC class I on dendritic cells
test.explain: CD40L on activated helper T cells binds CD40 on B cells; its deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome.

test.q: What cells do activated B cells become to secrete large amounts of antibody?
test.explain: Plasma cells are antibody factories.

test.q: The enzymes RAG1 and RAG2 drive V(D)___ recombination.
test.explain: V(D)J recombination joins variable, diversity and joining gene segments to create diverse receptors.

test.q: Human MHC molecules are called what? (abbreviation)
test.explain: In humans, MHC genes are the HLA (human leukocyte antigen) genes.

kidTest.q: What do B cells make?
kidTest.explain: B cells make antibodies, sticky tags for germs.

kidTest.q: What do killer T cells do?
kidTest.explain: Killer T cells find and remove infected cells.

kidTest.q: Why do you usually not get chickenpox twice?
kidTest.explain: Adaptive immunity keeps a memory and fights back fast the second time.

kidTest.q: Is adaptive immunity faster or slower than innate immunity the first time?
kidTest.explain: It takes days to start the first time, but it is very precise.

kidTest.q: How does a vaccine help?
choices: It scrubs your teeth so germs slide off
It makes you grow much taller really fast
It shows your body the germ's 'wanted poster' safely
kidTest.explain: Vaccines teach memory without you getting sick.

kidTest.q: Antibodies are made by ___ cells.
kidTest.explain: B cells (as plasma cells) make antibodies.

advancedTest.q: A boy has recurrent bacterial infections, very high IgM and absent IgG, IgA and IgE. Most likely defect?
advancedTest.explain: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome from CD40L deficiency blocks class switching; patients are also prone to Pneumocystis.

advancedTest.q: A patient on natalizumab develops progressive focal deficits and white matter lesions without enhancement. Most likely cause?
choices: Multiple sclerosis relapse with no other cause possible
advancedTest.explain: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin-mediated lymphocyte entry into the CNS, impairing surveillance and allowing JC virus PML.

advancedTest.q: A patient on an anti-CTLA-4 drug develops headache, fatigue and low cortisol. Which immune-related adverse event fits best?
advancedTest.explain: Hypophysitis is classically associated with anti-CTLA-4 therapy and presents with headache and pituitary hormone deficits.

advancedTest.q: Somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation occur mainly in:
choices: Germinal centers of secondary lymphoid follicles
Bone marrow during the pre-B cell stage
advancedTest.explain: AID-driven somatic hypermutation and selection occur in germinal centers.

lessons.title: Hypersensitivity Reactions

levels.kid:
Sometimes the body's guards get too excited and attack something that is not really dangerous. This is called a **hypersensitivity** reaction, or an over-reaction.

An **allergy** is the most common kind. A person allergic to peanuts has guards that think peanuts are bad guys. When they eat one, the guards sound a giant alarm. They might get itchy bumps, a runny nose, or a swollen face.

A very big alarm is called **anaphylaxis**. It can make breathing hard. That is an emergency, and grown-ups use a special shot called an **EpiPen** and call for help right away.

Other over-reactions are slower, like the itchy rash from poison ivy that shows up a day or two later.
levels.hs:
**Hypersensitivity** reactions are immune responses that cause harm instead of protection. They are grouped into four types (the Gell and Coombs classification):

- **Type I, immediate (allergy)**: on first exposure, the body makes **IgE** against a harmless antigen like pollen, peanut or bee venom. IgE sits on **mast cells**. On re-exposure, the antigen cross-links IgE and mast cells release **histamine** within minutes, causing hives, sneezing, wheezing and swelling. The most severe form, **anaphylaxis**, can cause airway swelling and a dangerous drop in blood pressure.
- **Type II, antibody against cells**: IgG or IgM binds antigens on a person's own cells, leading to their destruction. Example: a blood transfusion with the wrong ABO type.
- **Type III, immune complexes**: antibody-antigen clumps deposit in vessel walls, kidneys and joints and trigger inflammation. Example: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
- **Type IV, delayed (T cell-mediated)**: no antibodies; T cells cause damage 48 to 72 hours later. Examples: poison ivy rash, nickel allergy, and the TB skin test.

A memory trick is **ACID**: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed.

Anaphylaxis is treated first with **epinephrine** injected into the thigh muscle, plus calling emergency services. Antihistamines alone are not enough.
levels.college:
**Type I**: sensitization involves Th2 cells (IL-4, IL-13) driving IgE class switching; IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils. Re-exposure causes cross-linking and degranulation. The **early phase** (minutes) is from preformed mediators: histamine and tryptase. The **late phase** (hours) involves newly synthesized leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4), prostaglandin D2, and recruitment of eosinophils and Th2 cells. Diseases: allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma, urticaria, food allergy, anaphylaxis. Serum tryptase drawn within a few hours supports a diagnosis of anaphylaxis.

**Type II**: antibody against cell-surface or matrix antigens. Mechanisms include:
- Opsonization and phagocytosis or complement lysis: autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, hemolytic disease of the newborn, acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
- Inflammation: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-type IV collagen, linear IgG on immunofluorescence).
- Receptor dysfunction without cell death: Graves disease (stimulating TSH receptor antibodies), myasthenia gravis (blocking acetylcholine receptor antibodies).
The **direct Coombs test** detects antibody or complement on red cells.

**Type III**: soluble immune complexes deposit where filtration occurs. Examples: SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa (hepatitis B-associated), serum sickness (fever, rash, arthralgia about one to two weeks after exposure to a foreign protein), and the localized **Arthus reaction**. Labs show low complement (C3, C4) and granular deposits on immunofluorescence.

**Type IV**: CD4 Th1 or Th17 cells activating macrophages (tuberculin reaction, granulomas), or CD8 cytotoxicity (contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes beta-cell killing). Severe drug reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and DRESS are T cell-mediated.

Some reactions are not hypersensitivity in the immunological sense: **mast cell activation without IgE**, such as vancomycin flushing reactions or opioid and contrast reactions, is pseudoallergic.
levels.phd:
The Gell and Coombs scheme from 1963 remains a teaching scaffold, but modern immunology has outgrown it in several directions.

First, type IV has been subdivided by effector program: IVa (Th1, macrophages), IVb (Th2, eosinophils, as in DRESS), IVc (cytotoxic T cells, as in Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis) and IVd (T cells recruiting neutrophils, as in acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis). This maps clinical phenotype onto mechanism.

Second, drug hypersensitivity revealed **HLA-restricted pharmacology**. Carriers of HLA-B*57:01 develop abacavir hypersensitivity; HLA-B*15:02 strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in some Asian populations. Mechanistic models include the hapten model (the drug covalently modifies self proteins), the **p-i concept** (direct pharmacological interaction with immune receptors), and the **altered peptide repertoire** model, in which abacavir sits in the HLA-B*57:01 peptide-binding groove and changes which self peptides are presented, so T cells see 'new self'. Pre-prescription HLA genotyping is a rare example of pharmacogenomics in routine practice.

Third, type I allergy is not merely an error. The 'toxin hypothesis' argues that type 2 immunity evolved to defend against venoms and noxious substances, which fits evidence that mast cells and IgE protect mice from lethal venom doses on re-exposure. The **hygiene** and **old friends** hypotheses, and the dual-allergen exposure hypothesis (skin exposure sensitizes, gut exposure tolerizes), reshaped peanut guidance after the LEAP trial showed early oral introduction greatly reduced peanut allergy in high-risk infants.

Fourth, MRGPRX2 was identified as a mast cell receptor mediating IgE-independent degranulation to cationic drugs such as some neuromuscular blockers and fluoroquinolones, explaining many perioperative pseudoallergic reactions.

Finally, the hypersensitivity types often coexist in one disease, as in SLE, which involves type II cytopenias and type III nephritis.
levels.expert:
**Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis**: acute onset involving skin or mucosa plus respiratory compromise or hypotension, or hypotension or respiratory compromise after a known allergen even without skin signs. Up to a fifth of cases lack hives, so do not wait for a rash. The first and only first-line drug is **intramuscular epinephrine** into the anterolateral thigh, repeated if needed; delay is the strongest predictor of death. Lay the patient flat (standing up suddenly has been linked to fatal cardiovascular collapse), give oxygen and fluids. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and do not treat airway obstruction or shock. Patients on beta blockers may be refractory; glucagon is the classic rescue. Observe for a biphasic reaction and discharge with an auto-injector and an allergy referral.

**Transfusion reactions**: fever, flank pain, hypotension and hemoglobinuria minutes into a transfusion means **stop the transfusion**, keep the line open, and recheck identity: ABO mismatch (type II) is usually a clerical error. Distinguish TRALI (lung injury within hours, non-cardiogenic edema) and TACO (volume overload, responds to diuretics). Anaphylaxis during transfusion suggests IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies.

**Drug allergy labels** are wrong most of the time: most patients labeled penicillin-allergic tolerate penicillin after formal evaluation, and delabeling improves outcomes by avoiding broader antibiotics. Distinguish IgE features (hives, angioedema, wheeze within an hour) from benign delayed rashes and from severe cutaneous reactions (mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering, fever, organ involvement), which mean never rechallenge.

**Neuro links**: myasthenia gravis and Graves disease are type II receptor diseases; antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) are leading causes of SJS/TEN and DRESS, so a new rash in the first two months of an antiepileptic deserves attention, and HLA-B*15:02 screening is recommended before carbamazepine in at-risk ancestry.

**Contrast reactions**: most are non-IgE; prior reaction is a risk factor, and premedication protocols exist, but they do not prevent all reactions.

keyPoints: Type I: IgE and mast cells, minutes (allergy, anaphylaxis)
Type II: antibody against cells or receptors (transfusion reaction, Graves, myasthenia)
Type III: immune complexes deposit, complement falls (SLE, serum sickness)
Type IV: delayed, T cell-mediated (contact dermatitis, TB test, SJS/TEN)
Anaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine first

test.q: Which antibody mediates type I hypersensitivity?
test.explain: Type I reactions are IgE-mediated; IgE bound to mast cells triggers degranulation.

test.q: Which reaction is type IV (delayed)?
test.explain: Contact dermatitis is T cell-mediated and appears 48–72 hours after exposure.

test.q: A transfusion with the wrong ABO blood type causes which type of hypersensitivity?
test.explain: Preformed antibodies bind antigens on the donor red cells, a type II (cytotoxic) reaction.

test.q: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an example of:
test.explain: Immune complexes deposit in glomeruli, activating complement; C3 is low.

test.q: What is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis?
test.explain: Epinephrine reverses airway swelling and shock; antihistamines are only adjuncts.

test.q: The main preformed mediator released by mast cells in an allergic reaction is:
test.explain: Histamine causes itching, vasodilation, increased permeability and bronchoconstriction.

test.q: Graves disease and myasthenia gravis are type II reactions in which antibodies:
choices: Bind receptors and change their function
test.explain: Antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor in Graves or block the acetylcholine receptor in myasthenia, without necessarily destroying cells.

test.q: The tuberculin (TB) skin test relies on which hypersensitivity type?
test.explain: It is a delayed T cell response read at 48–72 hours.

test.q: Which lab finding is typical of active type III disease such as lupus nephritis?
test.explain: Immune complexes consume complement, lowering C3 and C4.

test.q: What is the most severe, life-threatening type I reaction called?
test.explain: Anaphylaxis is a systemic type I reaction with airway and/or circulatory compromise.

test.q: The memory trick for the four types is ACID: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, ___.
test.explain: Type IV is delayed, T cell-mediated hypersensitivity.

test.q: Which test detects antibody or complement already bound to a patient's red cells? (name the test)
test.explain: The direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test detects in vivo coating of red cells, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

kidTest.q: An allergy happens when the body's guards:
choices: Turn bright green like a leaf
Fall asleep for a long time
kidTest.explain: The guards treat a harmless thing, like pollen, as a bad guy.

kidTest.q: A big, dangerous allergy that makes breathing hard is called:
kidTest.explain: Anaphylaxis is an emergency.

kidTest.q: What should happen first if someone has anaphylaxis?
choices: Wait a while and see what happens
Give them a cookie and a nap
Use an EpiPen and call for help
kidTest.explain: Epinephrine and emergency help come first.

kidTest.q: Which of these is a common allergy trigger?
kidTest.explain: Peanuts, pollen and bee stings are common triggers.

kidTest.q: Poison ivy rash shows up:
kidTest.explain: It is a slow, delayed over-reaction.

kidTest.q: An itchy reaction from guards over-reacting to pollen is called an ___.
kidTest.explain: That is an allergy.

advancedTest.q: Before prescribing abacavir, testing for which allele prevents a T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction?
advancedTest.explain: HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity; abacavir alters the peptides presented by that HLA. HLA-B*15:02 is linked to carbamazepine SJS/TEN.

advancedTest.q: A patient on a beta blocker has anaphylaxis that does not respond to repeated epinephrine. Classic additional rescue drug?
advancedTest.explain: Glucagon raises cAMP independently of beta receptors and is the classic adjunct in beta-blocker-refractory anaphylaxis.

advancedTest.q: Minutes into a transfusion, a patient with no prior reactions develops anaphylaxis. Underlying condition to suspect?
advancedTest.explain: IgA-deficient patients can make anti-IgA antibodies that react to IgA in donor plasma.

advancedTest.q: Fever, rash with mucosal erosions and skin pain three weeks after starting carbamazepine most likely represents:
choices: Type IVc (cytotoxic T cell) reaction: SJS/TEN
advancedTest.explain: SJS/TEN is a cytotoxic T cell-mediated reaction; stop the drug and never rechallenge.

lessons.title: Autoimmunity

levels.kid:
Your immune guards are trained to fight germs and leave your own body alone. They learn the difference between 'me' and 'not me'.

Sometimes the guards get confused and start attacking parts of your own body. That is called **autoimmunity**. 'Auto' means 'self'.

What happens depends on what part they attack. If they attack the cells that make insulin, a person gets **type 1 diabetes** and needs insulin every day. If they attack the joints, the joints get sore and swollen.

Doctors can't always say why the guards get confused. Genes and things like infections may play a part. Medicines can calm the guards down so the body hurts less.
levels.hs:
**Autoimmune diseases** happen when the immune system loses **self-tolerance** and attacks the body's own tissues. They affect roughly 5 to 8 percent of people and are more common in women.

They can be:
- **Organ-specific**, hitting one organ: type 1 diabetes (insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas), Hashimoto thyroiditis (thyroid, causing low thyroid hormone), Graves disease (antibodies that overstimulate the thyroid), myasthenia gravis (nerve-muscle junction), multiple sclerosis (myelin in the brain and spinal cord).
- **Systemic**, hitting many organs: **systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)**, which can affect skin (the butterfly rash on the cheeks), joints, kidneys, blood cells and brain; **rheumatoid arthritis**, which attacks joint linings symmetrically, especially the small joints of the hands.

Why does tolerance fail? Usually a combination of **genes** (certain HLA types raise risk), **environmental triggers** such as infections, smoking or certain drugs, and **hormones**.

Doctors diagnose autoimmunity with symptoms, exams and blood tests for **autoantibodies**, such as ANA (antinuclear antibodies) in lupus.

Treatments usually calm the immune system: steroids, other immunosuppressants, and targeted biologic drugs. Some treatments replace what was lost instead, like insulin in type 1 diabetes or thyroid hormone in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
levels.college:
**Mechanisms of tolerance**: central tolerance (thymic negative selection, guided by AIRE; B cell receptor editing in marrow) and peripheral tolerance (anergy from lack of costimulation, Treg suppression, activation-induced cell death via Fas-FasL). Defects map to rare monogenic diseases: **AIRE** mutation causes APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy with candidiasis), **FOXP3** mutation causes IPEX, and **Fas** mutation causes autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

**Triggers**:
- **Molecular mimicry**: rheumatic fever (antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin), Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni (lipooligosaccharide mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides).
- **Epitope spreading** and release of sequestered antigens after tissue damage.
- **Drugs**: drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid; anti-histone antibodies, kidneys and brain usually spared).

**HLA associations**: HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis), HLA-DR3 and DR4 (type 1 diabetes), HLA-DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 (celiac disease), HLA-DR2/DR15 (multiple sclerosis).

**Key autoantibodies**:
- SLE: ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific; anti-dsDNA tracks nephritis activity).
- Rheumatoid arthritis: rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (anti-CCP more specific).
- Sjogren: anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB); anti-Ro in pregnancy risks neonatal heart block.
- Systemic sclerosis: anti-Scl-70 (diffuse), anti-centromere (limited, CREST).
- Celiac: anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA.
- Myasthenia gravis: anti-acetylcholine receptor or anti-MuSK.
- Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: c-ANCA (PR3).

**Treatment principles**: glucocorticoids for flares; steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate); hydroxychloroquine as the backbone in SLE; biologics against TNF, IL-6, IL-17, CD20 and B cell survival factors; and replacement of lost function in organ-specific disease.
levels.phd:
Autoimmunity is best viewed as a threshold phenomenon: polygenic risk, environmental exposures and stochastic events in lymphocyte selection push the system across a tipping point. Genome-wide association studies have mapped hundreds of risk loci, the strongest consistently in the **MHC**, but most non-HLA variants are non-coding and enriched in enhancers active in T cells and other immune cells, suggesting altered gene regulation rather than broken proteins. **PTPN22** R620W, which alters TCR and BCR signaling thresholds, links rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes and SLE.

The female bias (about 9 to 1 in SLE) has several explanations: TLR7 escapes X inactivation in a proportion of female immune cells, raising sensing of nucleic acids, while sex hormones modulate B cell selection. Gain-of-function TLR7 variants alone can cause childhood lupus.

SLE illustrates the role of debris handling. Deficiencies of early classical complement components (C1q, C2, C4) strongly predispose to lupus, because complement normally clears apoptotic cells; nuclear antigens persisting in the extracellular space are taken up by plasmacytoid dendritic cells via TLR7 and TLR9, producing a type I interferon signature that fuels autoreactive B cells. The anti-type I interferon receptor antibody anifrolumab validates the model.

The gut microbiome influences autoimmunity: segmented filamentous bacteria induce Th17 cells in mice, and germ-free animals are protected from some arthritis and CNS autoimmunity models.

Multiple sclerosis shows how epidemiology finds causes. A longitudinal military cohort found that Epstein-Barr virus infection increased MS risk about 32-fold and preceded rises in neurofilament light chain, supporting EBV as a likely necessary but insufficient cause; one proposed mechanism is mimicry between EBNA1 and the glial protein GlialCAM.

Finally, CAR-T cells targeting CD19 have produced drug-free remissions in refractory SLE, suggesting that a full reset of the B cell compartment can restore tolerance.
levels.expert:
**Approach**: the ANA is a screening test with high sensitivity and low specificity for SLE. Low-titer ANA is common in healthy people, especially older women, so ordering it for vague fatigue produces false positives and anxiety. Order it when the pretest probability is real: inflammatory arthritis, photosensitive rash, serositis, cytopenias, proteinuria or unexplained neuropsychiatric features. A negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely.

**Red flags** that change urgency: active urinary sediment with rising creatinine (lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease) needs rapid nephrology input and often biopsy; new vision loss with headache and jaw claudication in an older adult means giant cell arteritis, so start steroids immediately rather than waiting for the biopsy; pulmonary-renal syndrome (hemoptysis plus renal failure) is an emergency.

**Neurologic autoimmunity** matters for a future neurosurgeon:
- Multiple sclerosis: relapsing deficits separated in time and space, periventricular and juxtacortical lesions, CSF oligoclonal bands.
- Neuromyelitis optica: anti-aquaporin-4 antibody, severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis; MS drugs can worsen it, so test.
- Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ptosis and diplopia; watch for crisis with respiratory failure, and screen for thymoma with chest imaging.
- Autoimmune encephalitis: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in young people presents with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias and autonomic instability; look for an ovarian teratoma.
- Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness with areflexia after an infection; monitor vital capacity.

**Treatment pitfalls**: long-term glucocorticoids need bone protection, glucose and blood pressure monitoring, and consideration of Pneumocystis prophylaxis at high cumulative exposure. Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before biologics and anti-CD20 therapy. Hydroxychloroquine requires periodic retinal screening. Also remember autoimmune clustering: a patient with one autoimmune disease has a higher chance of another (type 1 diabetes with celiac or thyroid disease).

keyPoints: Autoimmunity is a failure of self-tolerance
Organ-specific (type 1 diabetes, MS, myasthenia) vs systemic (SLE, RA)
Genes (HLA), environment (infection, smoking, drugs) and sex hormones interact
Autoantibodies help diagnosis: ANA sensitive, anti-dsDNA/Smith specific for SLE, anti-CCP for RA
Treatment calms the immune system or replaces lost function

test.q: Autoimmunity is best defined as:
choices: Loss of self-tolerance so the immune system attacks the body's own tissues
A shortage of white blood cells, so infections happen more easily than usual
An infection by a virus that destroys the body's own immune cells over time
An allergy to pollen or dust, where the immune system overreacts to harmless things
test.explain: Autoimmune disease results from failed self-tolerance.

test.q: Which disease destroys insulin-producing beta cells?
test.explain: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells; type 2 is mainly insulin resistance.

test.q: Which antibody is highly specific for SLE and tracks nephritis activity?
test.explain: Anti-dsDNA (and anti-Smith) are specific for SLE; anti-dsDNA levels correlate with renal disease.

test.q: Which antibody is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
test.explain: Anti-CCP is more specific than rheumatoid factor for rheumatoid arthritis.

test.q: Anti-histone antibodies suggest:
test.explain: Drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid) typically has anti-histone antibodies.

test.q: HLA-B27 is most associated with:
test.explain: HLA-B27 is linked to ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies.

test.q: Rheumatic fever after strep throat is a classic example of:
test.explain: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with heart proteins.

test.q: Which feature is typical of rheumatoid arthritis?
choices: Symmetric small joints of the hands
Single big toe joint with tophi
Migratory large joints after a tick bite
test.explain: Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis of small joints (wrists, MCPs, PIPs).

test.q: Autoimmune diseases as a group are:
choices: Equally common in men and women
test.explain: Most autoimmune diseases are more common in women; SLE is roughly 9:1 female.

test.q: Which screening autoantibody test is very sensitive for SLE? (abbreviation)
test.explain: ANA is sensitive but not specific; a negative ANA makes SLE unlikely.

test.q: Celiac disease is screened with IgA anti-tissue ___ antibodies.
test.explain: Anti-tTG IgA is the standard screening test for celiac disease.

test.q: Mutations in which gene cause failure of thymic self-antigen expression (APECED)?
test.explain: AIRE drives expression of tissue-specific self proteins in the thymic medulla for negative selection.

kidTest.q: 'Auto' in autoimmunity means:
kidTest.explain: Auto means self: the guards attack your own body.

kidTest.q: In autoimmunity, the guards attack:
kidTest.explain: They get confused about 'me' and 'not me'.

kidTest.q: Type 1 diabetes happens when guards attack cells that make:
kidTest.explain: Without insulin-making cells, people need insulin every day.

kidTest.q: Can medicine help calm the guards down?
kidTest.explain: Medicines can calm the immune system.

kidTest.q: If guards attack joints, the joints get:
kidTest.explain: Inflamed joints hurt and swell.

kidTest.q: When guards attack the body's own parts, it is called auto___.
kidTest.explain: That is autoimmunity.

advancedTest.q: A young woman develops psychiatric symptoms, then seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and autonomic instability. Which test and search are most important?
choices: HLA-B27 testing and MRI of the spine and sacroiliac joints
CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies and imaging for ovarian teratoma
Serum IgE level and skin prick testing for common allergens
Anti-CCP antibodies and X-rays of the hands and wrists
advancedTest.explain: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is often paraneoplastic with ovarian teratoma; tumor removal plus immunotherapy is key.

advancedTest.q: A patient labeled MS has severe bilateral optic neuritis and a spinal cord lesion spanning many vertebral segments. Before starting MS therapy, test for:
advancedTest.explain: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is aquaporin-4 antibody-mediated, and some MS therapies can worsen it.

advancedTest.q: Deficiency of which complement components most strongly predisposes to SLE?
choices: Factor H of the alternative pathway
advancedTest.explain: Early classical complement clears apoptotic debris; deficiency drives nuclear-antigen exposure and lupus.

advancedTest.q: An older adult with new headache, jaw claudication and transient vision loss. Best next step?
choices: Order an ANA and wait for results before treating the headache
Prescribe antibiotics for a likely dental or sinus infection
Wait for the temporal artery biopsy result before starting treatment
Start glucocorticoids immediately, then arrange temporal artery biopsy
advancedTest.explain: Giant cell arteritis threatens permanent blindness; steroids should not be delayed, and the biopsy remains informative for days to weeks.

lessons.title: Immunodeficiency

levels.kid:
Imagine your body's security team is missing some guards, or the guards are too tired to work. That is called **immunodeficiency**. 'Deficiency' means 'not enough'.

Some kids are born with a weak team. They get sick again and again, with infections that most kids beat easily.

Other people lose guards later in life. A virus called **HIV** can attack the helper guards. Some strong medicines, like those for cancer, can also make the guards weak for a while.

Doctors help by giving medicine to fight germs, extra antibodies, and sometimes a new set of blood-making cells from a donor. People with weak guards also try hard to avoid germs, like washing hands a lot.
levels.hs:
**Immunodeficiency** means part of the immune system is missing or not working, so infections become more frequent, more severe, unusual, or hard to clear.

There are two broad kinds:
- **Primary** immunodeficiencies are genetic and usually show up in childhood. Examples: **X-linked agammaglobulinemia** (boys with no B cells and almost no antibodies), **DiGeorge syndrome** (the thymus does not develop, so T cells are low), and **severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)**, in which both B and T cell immunity fail; it is often called 'bubble boy' disease.
- **Secondary** (acquired) immunodeficiencies are far more common: **HIV/AIDS**, cancer chemotherapy, long-term steroids, transplant drugs, malnutrition, diabetes, and removal of the spleen.

The type of infection is a clue to what is broken:
- Antibody (B cell) problems: repeated bacterial infections of the ears, sinuses and lungs.
- T cell problems: viruses, fungi and unusual organisms such as **Pneumocystis** pneumonia.
- Neutrophil problems: skin abscesses and fungal infections.
- Complement problems: Neisseria (meningitis).
- No spleen: overwhelming infection by bacteria with capsules, such as pneumococcus.

Warning signs include many ear infections a year, two or more pneumonias, poor growth in a baby, and needing IV antibiotics to clear infections. Treatment depends on the cause: antibody replacement, antibiotics to prevent infection, or a bone marrow (stem cell) transplant.
levels.college:
**B cell (humoral) defects** typically appear after about 6 months, once maternal IgG wanes:
- **X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia**: BTK mutation, absent B cells, absent tonsils and lymph nodes, recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria and enteroviral meningoencephalitis. Avoid live vaccines.
- **Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID)**: low IgG and IgA or IgM with poor vaccine responses, usually diagnosed in adults; increased autoimmunity and lymphoma.
- **Selective IgA deficiency**: the most common primary immunodeficiency, often asymptomatic; sinopulmonary and Giardia infections; anaphylaxis to blood products.

**T cell defects**:
- **DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion)**: failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches: absent thymus, hypocalcemia from absent parathyroids, conotruncal heart defects (CATCH-22).
- **Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome**: STAT3 mutation, impaired Th17: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, eczema, high IgE.
- Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis: Th17 or AIRE defects.

**Combined**:
- **SCID**: X-linked IL-2 receptor common gamma chain (most common), adenosine deaminase deficiency, RAG defects. Absent thymic shadow, low TRECs on newborn screening, failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, thrush, opportunistic infections. Treat with hematopoietic stem cell transplant; avoid live vaccines and use irradiated blood.
- **Wiskott-Aldrich**: WAS gene, X-linked: thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, recurrent infections.
- **Ataxia-telangiectasia**: ATM DNA-repair defect: cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, IgA deficiency, malignancy and radiation sensitivity.

**Phagocyte defects**: chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase; abnormal dihydrorhodamine test; catalase-positive organisms), leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Chediak-Higashi (LYST: giant granules, albinism, neuropathy).

**Secondary causes** dominate in practice: HIV, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, glucocorticoids, splenectomy, diabetes, and protein-losing states.
levels.phd:
The pattern of infections in inborn errors of immunity has been one of the most powerful tools for mapping which immune pathway protects against which microbe, a reverse-genetics approach in humans.

Casanova and colleagues described **Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease**: patients with mutations in the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis (IL12RB1, IFNGR1, STAT1 loss of function) suffer disseminated infection after BCG vaccination or from environmental mycobacteria, yet handle most other pathogens normally. This exposed a narrow, non-redundant circuit. Likewise, defects in TLR3 signaling (UNC93B1, TLR3, TRIF) produce herpes simplex encephalitis in otherwise healthy children, because neurons and glia rely on cell-intrinsic TLR3-driven interferon, not systemic immunity, against HSV in the brain.

COVID-19 extended this logic: inborn errors of type I interferon immunity and, strikingly, **neutralizing autoantibodies against type I interferons** were found in a meaningful fraction of critical pneumonia cases, especially in older men. Here, autoimmunity creates immunodeficiency, a phenocopy of the genetic defect.

Genotype and phenotype do not map cleanly. Incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, somatic reversion mutations (seen in Wiskott-Aldrich and ADA-SCID, in which a reverted cell lineage gains selective advantage) and gain-of-function versus loss-of-function alleles in the same gene (STAT1 GOF causes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis; LOF causes mycobacterial susceptibility) complicate prediction.

Therapeutically, the field leads gene therapy: early gamma-retroviral SCID-X1 trials cured patients but caused leukemias through insertional activation of LMO2, which pushed the field toward self-inactivating lentiviral vectors and, more recently, base and prime editing. ADA-SCID gene therapy and enzyme replacement illustrate stepwise progress. Newborn screening with T cell receptor excision circles allows transplant before infection, which strongly improves survival.
levels.expert:
**When to suspect primary immunodeficiency**: infections that are severe, persistent, unusual or recurrent (the SPUR mnemonic), especially with failure to thrive, family history, or complications from live vaccines. But most children with frequent colds are normal: daycare toddlers commonly have many viral infections a year. The pattern matters more than the count.

**Pragmatic first-line workup**: complete blood count with differential (lymphopenia in infants is a SCID red flag; neutrophil count and morphology; platelet size), quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) with age-specific ranges, vaccine antibody titers (tetanus, pneumococcal) to test function, HIV testing, and CH50 if Neisseria. Second line: lymphocyte subsets by flow cytometry, dihydrorhodamine test, genetic panels.

**Management**: immunoglobulin replacement for antibody failure, with trough levels and infection frequency guiding adequacy; prophylactic antibiotics; avoid live vaccines in significant T cell or combined defects; irradiated, CMV-safe blood products for SCID; early stem cell transplantation.

**Secondary immunodeficiency is your daily reality**: chemotherapy neutropenia (febrile neutropenia protocol), transplant recipients (CMV, BK virus, Pneumocystis, Nocardia, Listeria), glucocorticoid-treated patients (Pneumocystis prophylaxis in those on prolonged high-dose steroids, especially with other immunosuppressants), and asplenic patients (vaccinate, educate, and give a standby antibiotic plan; overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can kill within hours).

**Neurosurgical angle**: brain abscesses or ring-enhancing lesions in an immunocompromised host broaden the differential: toxoplasmosis and primary CNS lymphoma in advanced HIV, Nocardia and Aspergillus in transplant recipients, and Listeria rhombencephalitis. Corticosteroids given for tumor edema can unmask infection and can blunt the diagnostic yield of lymphoma biopsy, so coordinate timing before giving them. Recurrent bacterial meningitis should prompt a search for a CSF leak (skull base defect), complement deficiency, or asplenia.

keyPoints: Primary (genetic) immunodeficiencies are rare; secondary (HIV, chemo, steroids, asplenia) are common
Infection type points to the defect: antibody = sinopulmonary bacteria, T cell = viruses, fungi, Pneumocystis
Complement deficiency = Neisseria; asplenia = encapsulated bacteria
SCID needs early stem cell transplant; avoid live vaccines
Severe, persistent, unusual or recurrent infections should trigger a workup

test.q: Which infection pattern suggests an antibody (B cell) deficiency?
choices: Recurrent bacterial sinus, ear and lung infections
test.explain: Antibody defects cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria.

test.q: Which is the most common primary immunodeficiency?
test.explain: Selective IgA deficiency is common and often asymptomatic.

test.q: DiGeorge syndrome involves absence of the:
test.explain: 22q11.2 deletion disrupts the 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches: no thymus (low T cells) and no parathyroids (low calcium).

test.q: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia is caused by a mutation in:
test.explain: BTK is required for B cell maturation; patients have almost no B cells or antibodies.

test.q: Chronic granulomatous disease leads to recurrent infections with:
choices: Catalase-positive organisms such as Staph aureus and Aspergillus
Viruses, especially herpes viruses and cytomegalovirus
test.explain: Without NADPH oxidase, phagocytes cannot kill catalase-positive organisms that neutralize their own peroxide.

test.q: After removal of the spleen, patients are most at risk from:
choices: Kidney stones from high calcium in the urine
Head lice and other skin infestations in school
Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
Food allergies that develop after the spleen is gone
test.explain: The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria; asplenic patients need vaccination and an urgent plan for fever.

test.q: Which is the most common cause of immunodeficiency worldwide?
choices: Chediak-Higashi syndrome, a lysosomal trafficking defect
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked platelet and T cell disorder
Secondary (acquired) causes such as HIV, malnutrition and drugs
SCID, a severe combined defect of T and B lymphocytes
test.explain: Acquired immunodeficiency is far more common than inherited forms.

test.q: Pneumocystis pneumonia most strongly suggests a problem with:
test.explain: Pneumocystis is a classic opportunist in T cell deficiency, including advanced HIV.

test.q: Why do babies with B cell defects often stay well for the first few months?
choices: Maternal IgG from the placenta protects them
Breast milk contains B cells that settle permanently
Their skin barrier is more mature at birth
test.explain: Transplacental maternal IgG wanes around 6 months, unmasking antibody deficiency.

test.q: Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema and recurrent infections in a boy suggests:
test.explain: Wiskott-Aldrich is X-linked: WATER mnemonic (Wiskott-Aldrich: Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections).

test.q: What does SCID stand for?
test.explain: In SCID both T and B cell immunity fail; stem cell transplant is curative.

test.q: Patients with severe T cell or combined defects should avoid ___ vaccines.
test.explain: Live attenuated vaccines can cause disseminated disease in severe immunodeficiency.

test.q: Which test screens for chronic granulomatous disease? (name the test, two words or abbreviation)
test.explain: The DHR flow test measures neutrophil oxidative burst; it is abnormal in CGD.

kidTest.q: Immunodeficiency means the guards are:
kidTest.explain: Deficiency means not enough.

kidTest.q: A person with weak guards gets sick:
kidTest.explain: Infections happen more often and can be worse.

kidTest.q: Which virus attacks the helper guards?
kidTest.explain: HIV attacks helper T cells.

kidTest.q: Can some strong cancer medicines weaken the guards for a while?
kidTest.explain: Chemotherapy can lower immune cells for a while.

kidTest.q: What simple habit helps people with weak guards avoid germs?
kidTest.explain: Handwashing removes many germs.

kidTest.q: Not having enough guards is called immuno___.
kidTest.explain: That is immunodeficiency.

advancedTest.q: A newborn screen shows very low TRECs. What does this suggest, and what is the priority?
choices: Iron deficiency anemia; start oral iron and recheck the screen at the two-month visit
A normal finding in newborns, since T cells mature after the first year of life
Selective IgA deficiency; no action is needed and live vaccines can be given on schedule
Possible SCID; confirm with lymphocyte subsets and plan early stem cell transplant, avoiding live vaccines
advancedTest.explain: Low T cell receptor excision circles indicate few new T cells, a SCID screen; early transplant greatly improves survival.

advancedTest.q: A previously healthy child develops herpes simplex encephalitis. Which inborn error is classically implicated?
choices: Defects in TLR3-interferon signaling in the CNS
advancedTest.explain: TLR3 pathway defects impair cell-intrinsic antiviral interferon in neurons and glia, causing HSV encephalitis.

advancedTest.q: A patient has recurrent bacterial meningitis with different pneumococcal strains and clear fluid dripping from the nose. What should you look for first?
choices: A CSF leak through a skull base defect
advancedTest.explain: CSF rhinorrhea through a skull base defect lets nasopharyngeal bacteria reach the meninges; recurrent meningitis should prompt this search.

advancedTest.q: Disseminated mycobacterial disease after BCG vaccination in an otherwise healthy child points to a defect in:
advancedTest.explain: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease reflects a narrow IL-12/IFN-gamma circuit.
